source_document.body:
J.B. Hunt Transport Services’ third quarter may prove to be a speed bump on the road to recovery. The company previously flagged significant cost pressures, some growth-related, heading into the Thursday print. To meet demand, some of its business units offered sign-on bonuses and increase driver recruitment spending. Some costs appear transitory, while others may linger through the end of the year.
J.B. Hunt ( NASDAQ: JBHT ) reported third-quarter revenue of $3.68 billion, which was 20% higher year over year and ahead of the $3.59 billion consensus estimate. Earnings per share of $1.82 were 6 cents higher y/y and 1 cent above analysts’ lowered expectations. (A higher tax rate was a 4-cent EPS headwind in the period, partially offset by a 2-cent decline in net interest expense.)
Table: J.B. Hunt’s key performance indicators – Consolidated
The company identified roughly $45 million in costs at an investor conference in mid-September. A sharp spike in diesel prices, driver hiring costs and elevated cargo claims forced the company to guide to a 5% to 10% sequential EPS decline in the third quarter (implying $1.77 at the midpoint of the range). The actual impact from the items totaled over $50 million in the period.
However, management told analysts on a Thursday evening call that “everything [is] playing out like a normal cycle,” noting it is common to incur incremental costs ahead of higher pricing and revenue.
“Any time that we see this pressure happening from a driver environment, [it] typically yields a much better pricing environment for the next bid season ,” said President and CEO Shelley Simpson.
The brunt of the cost-price mismatch likely occurred in August and September, and should fade as the magnitude of the cost pressure eases and recent contractual rate wins bleed through to results. It said office headcount was down 4.5% y/y in the period, as driver count increased 3.5%.
Fuel surcharges operate on a one-week lag. Diesel prices were up sequentially in nine of the 13 weeks of the third quarter. By month, retail diesel prices dipped 1% sequentially in July, but increased 10% sequentially in August and another 15% in September. The near-term headwind will become an earnings tailwind when prices revert.
The third quarter marked a fifth straight quarter of y/y improvement in operating income and EPS. The company’s earnings turnaround started in the 2025 third quarter, well ahead of peers.
Intermodal can exit 2027 operating within margin target range
Intermodal revenue increased 20% y/y to $1.83 billion as loads were up 8.5% and revenue per load increased 11%.
The period was up against an easier volume comparison to a year ago (-1%). By month, shipments grew y/y by 9% in July, 8% in August and 9% in September. Shipments increased 18% y/y in the East and 1% in the transcontinental network. Total intermodal carloads were up 6% y/y on the U.S. Class I railroads in the period (North American container moves were up 5% y/y).
Excluding fuel, revenue per load was up just 2% y/y. However, a 3% decline in length of haul, due to the mix shift to the East, was a modest headwind to yield metric. Management said it captured low-single-digit contractual rate increase in the 2026 bid season, which ended last month.
Table: J.B. Hunt’s key performance indicators – Intermodal
Sonar data shows the mode is currently 31% cheaper than truck, which is notably higher than the typical 10% to 15% discount carried in the East (approximately 25% in the West). Elevated truckload rates and record diesel prices remain ample tailwinds for road-to-rail conversion.
SONAR: Intermodal Contract Savings Index (IMCSI.USA). The IMCSI shows the savings percentage between domestic intermodal contract rate per mile and truckload contract rate per mile. The comparison includes fuel surcharges. To learn more about SONAR, click here .
Chart: (ORAILDOML.USA). The daily volume of intermodal containers moving in the United States, Canada and Mexico. The index is a 7-day moving average using the date that containers were in-gated at a point of origin. Intermodal trailers (trailer-on-flatcar) are excluded.
The unit booked a 91.9% operating ratio (inverse of operating margin ), which was 15 basis points worse y/y. Higher costs (driver personnel, equipment and employee benefits) led to an 11% increase in cost per load, offsetting the increase in yield.
The company’s container fleet was 92.1% utilized in the quarter, 170 bps better than in the second quarter and well ahead of the 83.6% utilization rate in the 2025 third quarter. However, average loads per container were down 1% y/y in the period, possibly due to a modest deterioration in rail service.
Improved rates and continued cost management could restore margins to the company’s long-term target range of 10% to 12% by the end of next year, management said.
Dedicated a Q3 cost victim
The dedicated unit’s OR deteriorated 360 bps y/y to 91.5%.
Revenue increased 11% y/y to $960 million as revenue per truck per week increased 10% and average trucks in service were up 1%. Revenue per truck was up just 3% excluding fuel. J.B. Hunt sold service on 425 trucks in the quarter (970 trucks year-to-date), but its pipeline remains at an all-time high.
Table: J.B. Hunt’s key performance indicators – Dedicated
Higher driver costs, group medical claims, insurance premiums and new account startup costs were among the headwinds in the quarter. It also incurred an elevated level of startup costs at new accounts. Average trailers in service increased 11% y/y even though loads grew just 3%.
It said it can revisit customer contracts and recoup incremental costs, like higher driver costs, before the annual rollover.
Brokerage books another profit
After 13 quarters operating in the red, the brokerage unit booked a second straight operating profit.
Revenue increased 57% y/y as loads grew 22% and revenue per load jumped 29% (inclusive of fuel). A 14.3% gross margin was 70 bps lower y/y but 180 bps better than the second quarter . Purchased transportation costs (spot rates) cooled following the Fourth of July. Loads per employee fell 5% y/y but gross profit per employee increased 17%. Headcount was 28% higher y/y.
Table: J.B. Hunt’s key performance indicators – Brokerage
The company’s asset-light TL unit returned to profit after a modest second-quarter loss. The $7-million operating profit was driven by a 29% y/y increase in revenue per load (excluding fuel) and a 4% increase in trailer utilization (loads per average trailer). The operating income result was roughly flat y/y.
Table: J.B. Hunt’s key performance indicators – Final Mile & Truckload
Shares of JBHT were down 3% in pre-market trading on Friday. The stock fell 14% from its mid-September earnings update to the Thursday close.
Why it matters? J.B. Hunt’s quarterly results serve as a bellwether for the intermodal, trucking and logistics industries. The company’s third quarter was a modest slowdown after four quarters of strong recovery. However, some of the incremental costs that plagued the period were likely transitory in nature.
